messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Adebayo was 18, single, and had started working as a tax consultant not long after leaving school, trying to keep his days structured and ordinary. That ordinary world was shattered during an assault in which he was raped, an experience that he described later in fragments rather than in a smooth account. What stayed with him most was not a verbal story but flashes: the shape of a room, the angle of a doorway, the sense of being trapped with a man whose presence he could not get away from. Even now, when he tried to speak about it, he said the memory came back mostly as pictures or images, and sometimes not as pictures at all but as a sudden wash of the same terror with no clear scene attached. He also noticed that when the memory surfaced he could still taste what he had tasted during the event, and that taste made the whole episode feel immediate again, as if it were happening in his mouth and body rather than in the past.

In the weeks after the assault, Adebayo began to treat shouting as dangerous. Raised voices, especially in the street or in the office, made his body tighten before he could think. A door slamming in the tax office or at home could send him into a jumpy alarm, and he described being especially unsettled when he was alone with men, even in ordinary situations that other people seemed to experience as neutral. Those moments did not merely remind him of what had happened; they made him feel that the danger was present again, and once that sense of threat took hold, his mind seemed to reach for the same terrifying pictures and bodily sensations he had been trying not to revisit. A sharp voice in a corridor or the sound of a door opening unexpectedly could bring back the visual fragments of the assault, and the taste memory would follow, making the past feel close enough to touch. When he found himself remembering in that way, the scenes became more potent, and the more vivid they became, the more he began to scan for the next sign that something bad was about to happen.

By the time he came for help, Adebayo had become constantly watchful. He was certain that strangers approaching him in ordinary settings were a threat, and he felt an immediate alarm if someone touched him unexpectedly, as if his body had decided before he did that contact meant harm. That sense of danger fed back into the way the memories returned: the more he braced for threat, the more the images and emotional intensity surfaced, sometimes without any clear picture at all, and the more he found himself noticing details that could signal risk. He would track men in waiting rooms, stiffen if someone stood too close, and flinch at a hand on his shoulder in the office. The everyday noise of his workplace became difficult to tolerate; a door opening too quickly or a colleague raising his voice would not only jolt him, but also bring on the same vivid fragments and taste that he associated with the assault. In turn, those memory bursts made him even more convinced that he had to stay on guard, and that conviction made the world feel full of possible attackers. He had started avoiding unfamiliar places because he felt he could not assess the danger there, and that avoidance had narrowed his life in practical ways: he turned down errands, kept to familiar routes, and became more dependent on predictable routines around work and home.

Adebayo finally sought therapy after noticing that the cycle was expanding rather than easing. He was tired of living as if every sudden sound, every door slam, every unexpected touch, and every unfamiliar man might signal the same violation repeating itself. What frightened him most was not only that the memories could come back so vividly, but that they seemed to train his body to expect danger everywhere, making even his office and his daily commute feel unsafe. He came hoping to stop feeling as though he were still inside the assault whenever a voice was raised or a stranger stepped too close, and hoping he could return to moving through the city, and his work, without fear taking over before he had a chance to think.
